strengths: The manuscript addresses an identifiable audience in high-dimensional classification and factor models. Sparsity of whitened mean differences offers an interesting alternative to sparsity of the discriminant direction, while allowing informative signal outside the leading principal components. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b10/review-experiment-drzwkvyk/call-82acd19058444d5ba605a21fac2f8c49/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Using entrywise eigenspace perturbation bounds to analyze estimated whitening is technically relevant. The explicit algorithms, discussion of related classifiers, and detailed proof decompositions make the proposed approach understandable.
The experimental design includes several covariance structures, relevant competing classifiers, 200 Monte Carlo replications with standard deviations, and two gene-expression applications.
weaknesses: Necessary correction: The QDA reduction in Eq. (5.9), and consequently Theorem 6, is invalid under the stated assumptions. Coordinates with zero whitened means can still contain covariance information. For example, take u=(0,1,…,1)/√(p−1), Σ1=puuᵀ+I, Σ2=puuᵀ+4I, μ1=e1, and μ2=2e1, with equal priors. These satisfy the intended QDA assumptions and give A0={1}. The reduced population rule uses only Z1, whose class distributions overlap, whereas the p−2 residual directions distinguish the variances and make the full Bayes error tend to zero. Additional structural restrictions or a different quadratic feature-selection rule are required; otherwise this extension must be removed.

Necessary correction: The proof does not establish the main consistency guarantee as stated. Theorem 3 assumes log p=o(n) and asserts almost-sure convergence of conditional classification risk. Section 8.4 instead obtains a bound involving √(log n log p/n), explicitly requires log n log p=o(n), and concludes convergence in probability of the discriminant-score difference jointly over training and test data. The stronger growth requirement and the missing argument for almost-sure conditional-risk convergence must be resolved. Theorem 5 inherits this gap.

Necessary correction: The elliptical-distribution extension overstates Bayes optimality. With unequal priors, the Bayes decision compares log h(q1)−log h(q2) with a prior-dependent threshold; monotonicity of h does not make this the Gaussian Fisher rule. Sub-Gaussian tails do not fix this issue. Sections 5.1–5.2 need appropriate restrictions, such as equal priors and a common decreasing radial profile, or a correctly derived decision rule.

Necessary correction: The simulation tables contain discrepancies that undermine confidence in the empirical evidence. For Model 2, the specified parameters give ||ζ||²=[10−100ρ/(1+19ρ)]/(1−ρ). Equation (3.1) therefore gives a Bayes error of approximately 0.0196% at ρ=0.9, whereas Table 3 reports an oracle error of 5.40%. Table 1 also repeats several results between ρ=0.7 and 0.8; its oracle error at ρ=0.8 is 0.19%, versus approximately 0.0221% analytically. These discrepancies require an audit of data generation, oracle implementation, and table transcription before the comparisons can be trusted.

Necessary qualification: The model-size tables compare counts in different representations. A small number of retained whitened coordinates generally requires all original variables because the whitening matrix is dense. Thus, selecting 12 whitened coordinates does not establish selection of 12 measured genes or a sparse classifier in the original inputs. Although Section 2.3 explains this distinction, the abstract, experimental conclusions, and model-size labels should consistently qualify the feature-selection claims.

Necessary clarification: The whitening estimator is specified inconsistently. On page 5, Λ̂ contains the leading eigenvalues of the sample covariance, but D̂=(Λ̂+σ̂²I)^(−1/2) adds the noise variance again. The corresponding population covariance eigenvalues already equal λk+σ². Resolve whether Λ̂ denotes covariance eigenvalues or noise-subtracted spikes, align the algorithm and proof identities, and state which estimator generated the experiments.

Optional improvement: Experiments varying n and p under exactly sparse whitened signals would help connect the numerical results to the theory. Sensitivity analysis for the 90% explained-variance rule would also be useful, since this practical choice need not recover the fixed spike count assumed in the analysis.
